transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a bit complicated, I suppose. I mean, I'm here because my daughter insisted, really, but I do know things haven't been quite right. Even on my better days—and I do have better days now, where the sadness isn't sitting quite so heavy on my chest, you know? But even then, I just can't shake this... this feeling. It's mostly at my church, St. Jude's, where I've been going for thirty years, and then also with the ladies in my Tuesday morning walking club. 

I just... I know they're watching me. I can feel their eyes on me when I walk into the fellowship hall, or when we're stretching by the park benches. And it's not just the looking. It's the things they do. Like the church bulletin on Sundays—I'll be reading it, just looking at the announcements for the bake sale or the choir practice, and there will be these little messages. Not my name, exactly, but phrases that are definitely about me, about things I've thought or done. And the walking club ladies, they'll be chatting about the weather or their grandchildren, but they slip these words into their sentences, these little coded messages meant for me to hear. I try to ignore it, I really do, I just keep walking or I just keep singing the hymns, but it's exhausting, always having to decipher what they're really saying about me. It just never stops, even when I'm feeling a bit more like myself.
When your mood is not low, do you still feel that people are sending you these messages about you?

Yes, doctor, that's exactly what happens. It's the strangest thing. You know, just a little while ago—maybe a month or two back, time sort of blends together for me lately—but there was a spell of several weeks where I was actually doing quite a bit better. I remember it clearly because I was finally getting up and getting properly dressed in the mornings. I wasn't just sitting around the living room in my housecoat and slippers until noon like I do when the sadness gets too heavy. I was actually putting on my nice slacks, the navy ones I bought at Macy's, and brushing my hair out properly. 

And I was eating a bit better, too! I started making myself a real breakfast again, a nice warm bowl of oatmeal with a little brown sugar and some raisins, instead of just staring at a piece of dry toast that I couldn't bring myself to chew. I really wasn't feeling so weighed down... that terrible, crushing feeling on my chest had lifted, almost like a fog had finally rolled out of the valley. 

But... well, even then. Even when I was feeling so much lighter and more capable, the other things didn't stop. I'd be standing right there at my kitchen sink, feeling perfectly fine, just washing my oatmeal bowl, and I would hear my name being spoken right there in my empty house. Just... someone saying my name, clear as a bell, when no one else was home. And then Sunday would roll around, and I'd go to St. Jude's feeling perfectly cheerful, not sad at all, but I still absolutely knew the people there were hinting about me. I could still hear it in the way they greeted me, the specific words they'd choose when they handed me the program, just constantly hinting at things I've done. It didn't matter at all that I was having a good few weeks and feeling like my old self. It's just so frustrating, because you'd think if the dark cloud lifts, everything else would go away too, wouldn't you? But it just stays right there with me.
Before these experiences began, did you have any major medical illness or injury to your brain?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I've had the usual things, you know, over the years. I had my appendix out when I was twenty-two, just after I married my late husband, Arthur. Oh, that was a dreadful scare, I thought it was just bad indigestion from the casserole I'd made, but no, it was the appendix! And I had a little trouble with my gallbladder about ten years ago, had to have that removed too. They do it with those tiny little incisions now, it's marvelous what they can do. But my brain? No, no injuries there. 

I've never been in a bad car accident or hit my head, thank goodness. Well, I did bump it on the open cabinet door last Tuesday when I was putting away the good china, but that was just a little knock, barely even left a bruise. And as for major illnesses, well, apart from the sadness, which is its own kind of illness, I suppose, I've been quite healthy. My blood pressure creeps up now and then, and Dr. Evans—he's my general practitioner, a lovely man, always asks after my daughter—he put me on a little white pill for that, but it's nothing major. No strokes or seizures or anything frightening like that. My mother, rest her soul, she had a terrible time with strokes towards the end, but I've been spared that, thankfully. So, no, nothing wrong with my brain in that sense, just... just this awful business with the messages and the voices.
For at least one full month, have the voices or these messages from others continued during a time when you were not depressed at all?

Well, yes, doctor, I... I thought I just explained that, didn't I? Maybe I didn't say it quite right. Sometimes my words get a little tangled up these days. But yes, absolutely, for a whole month, maybe even longer, like I was saying just a moment ago. 

It was that lovely stretch back in... oh, was it April? Or early May? The daffodils were just starting to come up along the walkway, the yellow ones Arthur planted all those years ago. They always cheer me up, those daffodils. And I was feeling so much better, not depressed at all, really. I was getting up, making my oatmeal, even went down to the garden center to look at some petunias. The sadness was completely gone, not a trace of it. I felt light as a feather! 

But the voices... and the messages... they didn't take a holiday. Not at all. Like I said, I'd be washing my bowl, feeling perfectly fine, and there it was—my name, spoken right out loud in the empty kitchen. And the ladies at the walking club, even when I was smiling and chatting and feeling just wonderful, they were still doing it. Still slipping those little coded words into their sentences about their grandchildren or the weather, making sure I knew they were talking about me. So yes, for at least a full month, maybe six weeks, I wasn't depressed one bit, but all that other awful business just kept right on going. It's so confusing, isn't it? You'd think one would have to do with the other, but they just seem to have a mind of their own.
Since these experiences began, have you found it harder to keep up with your usual daily activities, like managing the house, seeing people, or taking care of yourself?

Well, yes, it has been harder, if I'm being perfectly honest. I do still live at home, thank the Lord. I couldn't bear to leave my house, all my memories with Arthur are tied up in these walls. But... things have slipped. They really have. 

I used to be so active, you know. I had my quilting gatherings every other Tuesday down at the community center. We were working on a beautiful double wedding ring pattern for Sarah's—my neighbor's daughter—wedding gift. But I just... I stopped going. I couldn't concentrate on the stitches, and with the ladies there, I just felt they were looking at me sideways, slipping things into the conversation about the fabric choices that were really about me. So I stopped. And the walking club, too. I used to love our Thursday morning walks around the park, but I haven't been in months. It's just too exhausting trying to figure out what everyone really means when they say good morning. 

Even my gardening... oh, my poor garden. I used to spend hours out there pulling weeds and deadheading the roses. Arthur always said I had the greenest thumb in the county. But lately, I just look out the kitchen window at it. The weeds are taking over the daylilies, and I just can't seem to find the energy or the... the peace of mind to go out there and tend to it. 

And my daughter, Emily, bless her heart, she's noticed. She's a busy girl, works full time at the bank and has two little ones of her own, but she's started calling me every evening. Not just to chat, but to ask, "Mom, what did you have for dinner?" And she comes over on Sundays now to check my pill organizer, making sure I haven't missed any of Dr. Evans's blood pressure pills or missed any of my appointments. I feel terrible being a burden to her, I really do. I've always prided myself on being independent, keeping a tidy house and a full schedule, but... it's just all become so overwhelming lately. It's like wading through molasses just to get through a normal day.
